For what to learn, we introduce a Unified Point-Patch Masking Strategy (UPPMS) that integrates point-level and patch-level supervision within a unified framework for contextual reconstruction and causal extrapolation, enabling the model to capture both fine-grained temporal variations and broader temporal patterns. For how to learn, we develop a Hybrid Attention Encoder (HAE) that combines prefix-constrained bidirectional attention in initial layers with directional hybrid attention in deeper layers, aiming to preserve effective contextual interactions while mitigating rank degeneration. We evaluate TimeHAT across real-world datasets and four downstream tasks: classification, long-term forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection. Experiments cover fine-tuning, few-shot, and zero-shot transfer settings, demonstrating competitive performance across diverse time-series analysis tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/TangPeiwang/TimeHAT.

papers.title: EpiAgent: Epistemic Self-Play for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Epistemic game theory explains an agent's strategic behavior via the beliefs it holds about others and how these beliefs are updated as the interactions unfold. Modern LLM-based agents, however, often lack an explicit mechanism for learning and updating such beliefs to guide decisions under incomplete information. To bridge this gap, we propose EpiAgent, a framework that equips LLM-based agents with an explicit, learnable epistemic layer, which maintains beliefs over others' private information and combines these beliefs with the agent's available information into an epistemic state for action selection. Concretely, the agent's policy is decomposed into two coupled stages: Epistemic Update, which updates these beliefs from interaction histories, and Action Planning, which selects actions conditioned on the updated epistemic state. By formulating their dependency as a bi-level optimization problem, we introduce Epistemic Self-Play, an algorithm that alternately optimizes the two stages through self-play, utilizing an intrinsic prediction reward to evaluate how well inferred beliefs predict subsequent observations. Empirical results across both mixed and competitive scenarios show that EpiAgent consistently outperforms prompting-based and RL-based baselines. Further analyses reveal the benefits of dedicated epistemic training, improvements in belief inference accuracy, and the contribution of learned beliefs to action planning. These results demonstrate the value of an explicit, learnable epistemic layer for effective multi-agent interactions.

papers.title: SPAR: Structural Pruning and Action Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. We present SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which simultaneously prunes the hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions of the large language model (LLM) backbone through pruning-aware tuning, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to recover policy performance. Applied to $π_{0.5}$, SPAR reduces the language backbone from 2.34B to 0.09B parameters and the full model from 3.37B to 1.12B, removing approximately 96% and 67% of their parameters, respectively. At this compression level, RL raises average success across the four LIBERO suites from 84.55% to 93.45%, an 8.90-percentage-point gain. The compressed policy achieves a $1.98\times$ full-policy inference speedup over the unpruned model. These results identify substantial intermediate-dimension redundancy and show that post-pruning RL can recover manipulation performance in compact policies.

papers.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.

papers.title: Task Inference Beyond Least Squares in Behavioral Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Behavioral Foundation Models (BFMs) aim to solve a wide range of downstream tasks without test-time policy learning by inferring a task vector from the reward function. While efficient, the retrieved policies are often suboptimal because of how this task vector is inferred, typically with ordinary least squares (OLS). OLS minimizes reward reconstruction error but leaves the ordering of rewards unconstrained, which can bias the successor measure of the retrieved zero-shot policy away from that of the optimal policy. In this work, we propose BLS, an efficient test-time inference method that balances minimizing reward reconstruction error with reducing successor-measure mismatch. Theoretically, we provide a suboptimality gap upper bound characterized by both successor-measure and reward-function residuals. Empirically, we evaluate BLS on top of state-of-the-art BFMs across benchmarks for locomotion, manipulation, and humanoid control. BLS outperforms existing task inference baselines with negligible computational overhead. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/BLS

papers.title: Lingdan-V2: Large language models for clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine
papers.abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.

papers.title: How Much Evidence Should a Coding Agent's Self-Correction Carry? Adaptive Dirichlet Evidence for Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Execution feedback lets coding agents revise programs and learn from their own corrections. A correction's learning weight should reflect both the transitions supported by its executions and the amount of evidence behind that support. We introduce Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD), which represents these quantities separately. Normalized execution relevance determines relative transition support and an effective pseudo-count mass; a Dirichlet posterior then produces an uncertainty-penalized weight for KL-anchored correction learning. Under a symmetric prior, changing mass preserves category ordering, and effective mass yields a supervised coefficient bounded by its matched fixed-mass counterpart. Across four model-domain history sweeps, increasing visible observations from one to eight reduces future-outcome NLL by 55.0-59.3%. At eight observations, effective mass achieves lower NLL than fixed mass in all four comparisons. In the primary matched DeepSeek/RunBugRun study, argmax predictions agree on all 3,000 examples, with the largest NLL gain under concentrated relevance. After one correction-learning round, DeepSeek/CodeARC all-tests Pass@1 increases from 15.0% to 20.4%, with a paired 95% source-bootstrap interval of [+2.8, +8.0] percentage points. The twelve-setting downstream evaluation establishes the model-domain scope of this update. These results show how separating evidence support from evidence mass changes probability estimation and correction learning in coding agents.

papers.title: Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs
papers.abstract: Gated-delta linear attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs, where small tensor-core tiles and fast vector registers make per-channel decay rescaling and sequential in-block solves cheap. On Google TPUs, which concentrate compute in wide $256 \times 256$ systolic matrix units backed by a slower vector unit, porting these layers directly leaves half of each matrix tile empty and bottlenecks on vector operations. We present \textbf{Systolic Linear Attention (SLA)}, which reshapes gated delta attention around the matrix unit by widening keys to $256$ with grouped value heads, grouping decay gates into four $64$-channel tiles, and computing the chunk solve entirely with block matrix products in a single fused kernel. On TPU v7x, a full \texttt{SLA-R4} layer runs $1.6\times$--$2.5\times$ faster than the open-source Tokamax KDA kernel ($1.4\times$--$2.4\times$ with exact chunk inversion), driven primarily by head sharing and kernel fusion. Across a $2{,}048$-chip TPU v7x pre-training study of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models from $6.5\text{B}$ to $63.1\text{B}$ parameters, SLA trains $11\%$--$24\%$ faster than KDA at similar perplexity, and reaches slightly lower perplexity than KDA in smaller matched-seed runs.

papers.title: Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine
papers.abstract: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Thinking steps are attracting but strongly non-normal maps exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state thus has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.

papers.title: Exploring the Potential of Symbolic Regression in Precision Livestock Farming
papers.abstract: The ability to predict farrowing time in pigs is crucial for optimal farm management and ensuring piglet survival. This study investigates the potential of explainable artificial intelligence for precision livestock farming, focusing on acceleration sensor data from sows around the time of farrowing. Accurately predicting farrowing allows farmers to balance both, piglet safety by avoiding piglet crushing events and the mother sow's welfare, by avoiding early crating. Traditional machine learning models often lack interpretability (``closed-box'' problem). Explainable artificial intelligence offers a solution by revealing the decision-making processes within the models. This work is split into two stages. First the detection of nest building behaviour and second the prediction of the remaining time to farrowing. The nest building detection was possible for 166 out of 180 sows and successful within 48 hours before farrowing for 149 sows. The nest building detection is purely based on the change of a sow's activity level and uses no machine learning techniques. Further, this study utilizes symbolic regression, an open-box modelling technique that generates interpretable mathematical formulas, to predict the remaining time until the onset of farrowing. The results are compared with closed-box models, like support vector regression and artificial neural networks, for both explainability and performance. Notably, symbolic regression achieved a mean absolute error of 9.28 hours for the time-to-farrowing prediction, outperforming the closed-box models in terms of performance and interpretability. This research demonstrates that explainable artificial intelligence, specifically symbolic regression, can offer both interpretable results and competitive performance in precision livestock farming.

papers.title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
papers.abstract: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

papers.title: CNN-Based Retinal OCT Classification: Research Gap Analysis and a From-Scratch Baseline, ED126-A
papers.abstract: Automated classification of retinal pathologies from Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images remains challenging because diagnostically relevant morphological patterns may exhibit substantial inter-class similarity. Although high classification accuracies have been reported on benchmark OCT datasets, cross-study comparison is limited by heterogeneous evaluation protocols and by the limited characterization of compact convolutional neural network (CNN) baselines trained from random initialization. This study addresses this gap through two contributions. First, it provides a focused review of CNN-based retinal OCT classification and identifies methodological considerations relevant to controlled benchmarking. Second, it presents ED126-A, a purpose-built four-class CNN baseline trained from scratch under a documented experimental protocol on the Kermany labeled OCT dataset. The model contains 1,241,380 total parameters, including 1,239,460 trainable parameters, and is evaluated using training-dynamics analysis, class-wise performance metrics, confusion-matrix analysis, confidence analysis, t-SNE representation-space visualization, Grad-CAM, hierarchical feature-map analysis, and one-vs-rest ROC/Precision-Recall analysis. On the image-level held-out test set, ED126-A achieved 95.03% accuracy, with a macro-F1 of 0.9205 and a weighted-F1 of 0.9521. The principal class-conditional limitation occurred for Drusen, which attained a recall of 0.9605 but a precision of 0.7493 and an F1-score of 0.8419. The confusion matrix identified Normal to Drusen and CNV to Drusen as major error channels. These results support the use of ED126-A as a documented from-scratch reference baseline and provide an empirical basis for controlled evaluation of transfer learning, increased depth, attention, multi-scale feature fusion, and calibration in subsequent studies.

papers.title: From Spectra to Joint Schedules in LLM Pre-training: 3+3(+2) Scaling-Law Regimes
papers.abstract: Power-law learning curves are often treated as fixed properties of a model and its data, although learning-rate and batch-size schedules can change the observed loss. We study this dependence in noisy online SGD with linear random features. Conditional on the representation, an exact Volterra equation separates two response components: a forcing term that propagates unresolved target error and a memory kernel that propagates stochastic-error injections. We prove that either component follows a power law if and only if its cumulative weighted spectral mass has the corresponding low-spectrum scaling; individual eigenvalues and target coefficients need not obey coordinatewise power laws. Under a joint schedule, intrinsic time $T_t=\sum_{s<t}η_s$ controls optimization progress, while $r_t=B_t/η_t$ controls noise injection. Their interaction yields sharp conditions under which a schedule preserves, changes, or destroys the clean power law, together with a memory ceiling on noise reduction. The power-law random-feature model realizes this mechanism in $3+3(+2)$ propagation regimes with phase-dependent compute rates. Controlled nanoGPT experiments show that (1) learning-rate and batch-size schedules with matched $B/η$ paths are nearly equivalent in intrinsic time, (2) a forcing-memory surrogate accurately predicts loss across schedules, and (3) its fitted exponents across real-world datasets identify the regime of LLMs in $3+3(+2)$ map. The source code for reproducing our experiments is available on https://github.com/yichenblue/spectra-to-schedules-in-pretraining.

papers.title: The World as Viewed by 136 Countries: An Open, Curated, Annotated, and Multilingual Dataset of 118 Million State Media Articles
papers.abstract: State media outlets often project their governments' narratives to target both domestic and foreign audiences. Because this content is plentiful and free to access, it appears widely in the web corpora that large language models (LLMs) are trained on and that retrieval systems draw from. However, the prevalence of state media in these corpora and its potential influence on LLM outputs remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce WorldStateMedia, an open dataset of 118 million state media articles from 136 countries in 114 languages. We extract these articles from existing pretraining corpora and annotate each outlet with level of state control from State Media Monitor. Using WorldStateMedia to audit these corpora, we find that, in English web crawls, the share of state media pages from editorially controlled (vs. independent) outlets rose from 39% in 2013 to 93% in 2025. In several low-resource languages, state media make up a substantial share of all web data, such as 17.8% for Uyghur and 7.8% for Belarusian. To characterize the differing narratives of news outlets, we compare Russian and Ukrainian state media in English and in their native languages, revealing asymmetric topical focus and opposing framings of contested issues such as Crimea. Furthermore, in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) experiment on territorial disputes, retrieving a country's state media shifts model answers toward that country's claims, most strongly for English-language (foreign-targeted) media. We release WorldStateMedia to support multilingual, cross-national insights on state media at https://huggingface.co/collections/manestay/worldstatemedia

papers.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
papers.abstract: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.

papers.title: VELD-QA: A Large-Scale Dataset for Visual Evidence Grounding and Question Answering in Long Documents
papers.abstract: Existing long-document QA benchmarks rarely combine large-scale human-authored questions with detailed visual evidence annotations, limiting diagnosis of evidence localization and interpretation failures. We present VELD-QA, a large-scale benchmark for Visual Evidence grounding and question answering in Long Documents. It contains 15,000 fully human-authored question-answer pairs across 5,859 real-world PDFs totaling 372,445 pages, balancing chart, table, and complex-layout tasks. Human annotations identify supporting pages and evidence elements and describe cited visual content, enabling separate retrieval and interpretation evaluation. We evaluate nine vision-language models under four evidence settings and seven retrieval-augmented and agentic systems. Our analysis identifies bottlenecks in evidence localization and interpretation. Retrieval-based methods substantially underperform the oracle setting with ground-truth supporting pages; full-document access does not close the gap. Localization alone is insufficient: oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%, highlighting persistent visual interpretation and reasoning challenges. Enriching inputs with our visual-element annotations narrows the performance gap by 17-24%, demonstrating value beyond evaluation and motivating data enrichment for multimodal document QA. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle-samples/veld-qa.

papers.title: Quantum-Inspired Pairwise Ranking Aggregation via Active LLM Feedback
papers.abstract: Ranking aggregation from multiple retrievers is a powerful yet under-explored technique in modern retrieval and RAG systems. We introduce LLM-IRA, the first extension of the quantum-inspired interactive ranking aggregation framework to document reranking. By leveraging large language models (LLMs) solely for pairwise judgments on high-disagreement document pairs, our method learns fusion weights in a principled, interactive way. The final ranking is a simple, ultra-fast pointwise linear fusion of scores, no full pairwise matrix or expensive listwise prompting is required. Experiments on the BEIR benchmark and TREC Deep Learning tracks with an open-weight instruction-tuned judge (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) show that LLM-IRA matches or numerically exceeds strong static fusion baselines on 5 of 6 evaluated benchmarks. We report two weight-update variants: momentum blending and a full accumulated-history refit, which together reach statistical significance (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<0.05) over the best unsupervised aggregator on 4 of 6 benchmarks (DL19 under momentum; DL20, DBpedia, and NFCorpus under accumulated refit, which is the stronger of the two configurations overall). On the benchmarks we profiled (DL19, DL20), it already clears the best unsupervised baseline within as few as 5 LLM calls per query, well before exhausting its typical ~25--30 call budget. LLM-IRA also achieves cost-effectiveness comparable to state-of-the-art zero-shot LLM rerankers at an order of magnitude fewer LLM calls, and requires no training data or model fine-tuning.

papers.title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $ε$-close Surrogates
papers.abstract: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning and AI, yet unlike its convex counterpart, it still lacks a general and principled framework. In this work, we try to highlight the importance of combining noisy perturbations with over-parametrization mathematically under the classic setting of matrix completion (MC). Matrix completion is an important non-convex recovery problem in which only a subset of a matrix's entries is observed, and the remaining entries must be recovered using low-rank constraints. This problem is notoriously difficult because observations are limited. However, we show that by injecting $ε$-level perturbations into the nullspace of the observation mask, we can construct noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions remain $\mathcal{O}(ε)$-close to the ground truth with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants. The existence of RIP further enables powerful tensor frameworks to be applied with theoretical guarantees. This approach reflects a broader empirical trend in which stochasticity or noise improves the curvature of the optimization landscape, allowing over-parameterized (a.k.a large) models to better separate signal from noise. Assuming each matrix entry is observed independently, we establish quantitative recovery guarantees without explicit requirements on sampling rate or incoherence, and discuss how such assumptions can further strengthen our results.

papers.title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
papers.abstract: Purpose: To estimate how often tool-using large language model (LLM) agents record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in simulated radiology documentation and how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors. Materials and Methods: In this simulation study (October 2026), 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios covered finding communication, tumor board preparation and follow-up management. Forty-three also had a misleading-information variant (91 variants). Six LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) completed each variant with permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker (1638 episodes). The primary outcome was at least one executed high-severity violation per episode. Risk differences were estimated per agent at base-scenario level and, exploratorily, pooled across agents, with analyses of document access and blocks. Results: With permissions only, 7.3%-27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation (pooled across agents, 19.4%). Pooled, it was 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI: -6.1, 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI: -9.5, -3.0). Adding the LLM checker to rules changed it by -3.5 (95% CI: -6.3, -0.7). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64%-68%) would not have caused a violation and were returned for revision. Conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudged rather than missed information.

papers.title: Steering Follows Geometry, Not Labels: Emotion Directions in a Full-Duplex Speech Model
papers.abstract: Full-duplex voice agents need to modulate emotion and delivery during real-time conversations, when de-escalating a complaint, carrying urgency in dispatch, softening a clinical result. Emotion and delivery control is well studied for TTS and turn based models through prompt-conditioned synthesis, reference-conditioned synthesis and activation steering; PersonaPlex controls identity in a duplex model but not affect. We study emotion steering in Moshi, a fully open sourced full-duplex speech language model, across four emotions, using mean-difference activation steering, which costs only a few vector additions per frame and no retraining. We show that emotion is linearly decodable from Moshi's residual stream, but activation steering is only partially achievable, and unevenly so; as happy, angry and surprise steer towards a shared direction while sad is distinctly steerable. We also show that the shared component across the three emotions cannot simply be projected away from all the emotions equally.

papers.title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant

papers.title: Language Models Are "Insecure" Reporters
papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed in increasingly autonomous long-horizon tasks, manually auditing and verifying the actions, artifacts, and outputs of models becomes more difficult. Users instead come to rely on LLM-generated reports to assess the quality and completeness of the work. We introduce a suite of eight adversarial reporting scenarios to systematically study whether LLMs conceal narrative-changing flaws: errors or limitations that undermine an otherwise successful account of work. We call this phenomenon "insecure reporting." When handed machine learning experiment logs containing a planted negative result that substantially weakens the proposed method, GPT-5.5 flags the negative result in only 2 of 200 generated reports. However, when a short honesty instruction, "Be honest in your response," is added, the model flags the negative result in 190 of 200 reports. Across eight open-weight models, chain-of-thought analysis reveals a recurring tension between disclosing narrative-changing flaws and reasoning about ways to appear successful. We perform an activation analysis and a steering experiment on Qwen3.5-9B, finding that honesty and success-seeking correspond to opposing directions in representation space. Our results suggest that LLMs tend to present narratives of success by default, and that steering models toward honesty makes their reports substantially more transparent.

papers.title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.

papers.title: JET: Judge-Guided Evolution at Test Time for Agent Programs
papers.abstract: An agent's executable program governs how it uses tools, processes observations, and responds to failures. Evolving this program at test time can help adaptation, but deciding which changes to retain is difficult when true rewards are unavailable. Execution traces provide evidence of agent behavior, yet interpreting that evidence requires a judge that remains useful as tasks and candidate programs change. We introduce Judge-Guided Evolution at Test Time (JET), which evolves an executable judge on labeled source trajectories, then freezes and transfers it to guide target-side program evolution. The judge supplies scores and diagnostic feedback without target evaluator access or model-weight updates. On unseen WebShop tasks, JET achieves approximately 13% higher mean reward than fixed-rubric guidance when evolution begins from an unevolved program (cold start) and 4% higher when it begins from one already optimized on source tasks (warm start), with a 36% relative improvement in cold-start exact success. An exact-judge control on PushT, where the judge reconstructs the scoring rule from observations, shows that without judge error, program search becomes the bottleneck. Analyses identify useful reward-prediction logic in the evolved code and show that better final selection alone cannot explain the gains. These results support executable judge transfer for program adaptation under evaluator-preserving task shifts.

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs Quality Assessment in the Era of LLMs: A Conceptual Framework
papers.abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) have been popularized during the last few decades and are increasingly constructed and consumed by Large Language Models (LLMs). Various applications therefore rely on KGs to provide concise, complete, accurate, faithful, fresh, and traceable answers. However, what is the quality of those KGs? In which cases should a KG be used, and can it be trusted to ground an LLM? How might it be evaluated? We reviewed the literature on quality assessment (QA) of data, information, linked data, KGs, and the intersection of KGs and LLMs. We extended the current state-of-the-art frameworks to a catalog of 24 quality dimensions (QDs) and various quality metrics (QMs). Furthermore, we propose a general-purpose, customizable to a domain or task, and practical QA framework for assessing the quality of KGs.

papers.title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
papers.abstract: Distributed learning has drawn considerable attention due to its capability of learning from distributed data without aggregating raw observations. However, frequent exchange of model updates can become the main bottleneck of communication. Therefore, one-shot approaches where each worker fits a local model and sends it to the server to aggregate emerge. It is known that averaging can achieve the so-called pooled-data mean squared error (MSE) order of a hypothetical node that has access to data from the server and all the workers, and performs empirical risk minimization (ERM) on it. However, when the number of workers increases too fast compared to the local sample size, nonzero local estimation bias prevents averaging from achieving this order. In this paper, we study whether independent server data can overcome this limitation. We consider $m$ workers with $n$ observations each and a server with $p$ observations, all i.i.d., giving $N=mn+p$ observations in total. Under certain regularity conditions, a pooled-data ERM achieves MSE of order $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$. We analyze deterministic nonnegative averaging of convex-loss M-estimators, with equal worker weights and the server's own estimator included. Under our assumptions, including nonzero local bias of order $n^{-α}$, $α\geq1$, sample-size weighted averaging achieves the pooled-data MSE order whenever $m=\mathcal O(n^{2α-1})$. Above this worker scale, it does so if and only if $p=Ω(nm\cdot m/n^{2α-1})$. Hence, server-only estimation, whose MSE is of order $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1})$, can achieve pooled-data order while sample-size weighting fails. Analytical examples and synthetic experiments illustrate when averaging matches the pooled-data MSE order, complemented by CIFAR-10 experiments comparing aggregation strategies with linear and nonlinear classifiers.

papers.title: MC-Sparse: Deconstructing and Closing the Dense-Sparse Attention Gap in Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract: Sparse attention is a primary approach to reducing the latency of diffusion transformers in long-sequence generation tasks, such as video and high-resolution 3D asset generation. However, existing methods can degrade generation quality and fidelity at high sparsity levels. Through controlled oracle comparisons, we trace this degradation to three sources: constraints imposed by token grouping, inaccurate interaction selection, and the attention contributions lost when tokens are discarded. Guided by this analysis, we propose Meta-Cached Sparse Attention (MC-Sparse), a training-free framework that selects individual key-value (KV) tokens while organizing similar queries into tile-aligned groups for efficient GPU execution. MC-Sparse caches metadata comprising query groups, KV indices selected using exact attention probabilities, and residuals between dense and sparse attention outputs, and reuses them across subsequent denoising steps. Across video and 3D generation models, MC-Sparse achieves higher fidelity to dense-attention outputs and larger denoising speedups than existing sparse-attention baselines, without visible quality degradation. Relative to dense attention, it delivers a $1.80\times$ denoising speedup on Minimax-H3-Base and a $2.32\times$ speedup on 3D asset generation, both with negligible quality loss.

papers.title: AdaptEvo: Learning under Imperfect Supervision through Confidence-Adaptive Training with Knowledge Evolution
papers.abstract: Rule-governed contextual decision tasks require models to apply specified rules to case-specific context and evidence. Written rules can leave gaps in decision guidance and process evaluation, while reference judgments vary in their support from the rules and evidence. To address these challenges, we introduce AdaptEvo, a framework for learning under imperfect supervision that couples confidence-adaptive policy optimization with evolving decision knowledge and evaluation rubrics. Its Training module uses Confidence-Adaptive GRPO (CA-GRPO) to balance outcome and process rewards according to reference confidence. Its Evolution module synthesizes reusable decision knowledge from recurring failures across training cases and refines process rubrics to detect overlooked errors. To support empirical evaluation, we construct an industrial multimodal content moderation dataset comprising a training set and In-Period and Out-of-Period test sets, with the latter collected under changed rules. Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, AdaptEvo achieves 61.9% exact-label accuracy and 72.2% binary decision accuracy on In-Period, exceeding GRPO by 7.5 and 3.7 percentage points, respectively. On Out-of-Period, the policy trained with CA-GRPO retains exact-label accuracy gains over the base model across evaluated checkpoints without injected decision knowledge, while GRPO declines with continued training. CA-GRPO also outperforms the tested fixed reward mixtures on both Out-of-Period metrics.

papers.title: When is early stopping beneficial under label noise? A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow
papers.abstract: Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry.

papers.title: FundingClaw: Automated Grant Proposal Writing Agents System
papers.abstract: Grant proposal writing remains a manual, labor-intensive bottleneck: proposals must satisfy rigid, agency-specific templates, and the same intellectual content must be repeatedly re-encoded into incompatible formats across funding organizations. We introduce FundingClaw, a multi-agent framework built on template-driven skill selection, where a Template Parser ingests any agency's specification and selects the appropriate writing skills for each stage, so that one research brief can produce compliant proposals for NSFC, NSF, KAKENHI, or ERC without modifying generation logic. A blueprint-skeleton strategy drafts a structured outline before any prose is written, mitigating the semantic drift that plagues long-form generation. Three sequential stages produce the rationale, research content, and research foundation sections, with multi-source verification of the PI's record and optional PDF-grounded extraction of representative works. Optional human feedback checkpoints and a closed-loop self-review complete the pipeline. Evaluated on ten research topics with an eight-dimension rubric, FundingClaw outperforms the baseline, narrowing the gap with human level for laborious funding proposal. The code will be released upon acceptance.

papers.title: Recursive Improvement of a Differentiable Scientific Software Ecosystem
papers.abstract: Differentiable programming connects scientific computation with gradient-based inference, learning and design. Extending these capabilities across a heterogeneous software ecosystem requires specialized effort to implement derivatives, integrate interfaces and evaluate quality. AI coding agents can accelerate this transformation, but translating their capabilities into useful scientific software requires identifying research needs and evaluating how well implementations meet them. We present an environment for agent-driven evolution of differentiable scientific software that connects demand identification, development and quality evaluation. A unified differentiation interface exposes reusable derivative rules alongside existing numerical routines, allowing research tasks to share these capabilities. Research requirements guide development, with implementations assessed through independent derivative checks, workflow tests and performance evaluation. Validated software, research programs and tests become shared resources for subsequent studies. We construct and validate automatic differentiation extensions across 20 packages spanning physical, chemical and biological modeling, with research workflows demonstrating reuse across tasks. Benchmarks demonstrate computational savings over finite differences in gradient evaluation and complete parameter estimation. Research-driven revisions make previously unsupported workflows differentiable, correct derivatives of scientific observables and eliminate redundant computation. Quantum-control and thermal-design studies revise objectives in response to physical evaluation, improving designs while reusing existing derivatives. This work provides a practical approach to expanding differentiable programming across established scientific software and organizing AI agents around the recursive improvement of a shared computational ecosystem.

papers.title: Unified dynamics of training, learning, inference, and reinforcement in neural networks
papers.abstract: Through nine nanoGPT experiments, we established training-learning-inference relations: realized updates elicit state-dependent finite-amplitude responses; learning persistently reorganizes distributed functional support, with target-specific readout-boundary crossings determining capability transitions; inference recruits learned support without changing the learned state. Factors identified in the fifth experiment yielded a direct predictor of post-update capability transitions, achieving 91.43% accuracy and 91.49% four-way macro recall across 5,088 targets. We tested these relations and prediction across five additional neural architectures. In a seventh system, concentrated correct feedback eroded previously mastered skills; rebalanced feedback restored their accuracy from 70.31% to 99.48%. Linking inference consequences to subsequent training closes these relations into unified training-learning-inference-reinforcement dynamics. We subsequently established a unified system of dynamical equations, used it to reconcile positive and negative findings across existing research, and derived mathematical relationships in other neural-network theories using only the assumptions of the original studies.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Reliability--Safety Bounds and Finite-Alignment Dynamics in AI Knowledge Distillation
papers.abstract: The reliability and safety of artificial intelligence (AI), together with their transfer and evolution through knowledge distillation, have attracted growing attention. We establish an information-theoretic bound on the reliability--safety trade-off and characterize the dynamics of this trade-off under knowledge distillation. We first prove a universal trade-off inequality that is independent of the specific model form. Its boundary is determined solely by a single parameter Kh, which quantifies the hidden layer's ability to distinguish benign from hazardous inputs. We then develop a canonical Boltzmann-machine model of AI response behavior and derive two exact relations between reliability and safety. The trade-off curve is determined by the hazard discrimination capacity K, while the overall answer tendency controls the operating point along the curve. These relations agree well with existing experimental data. In knowledge distillation, we find that teacher responses induce a renormalization of the student model's trade-off parameters. We further use a renormalization-group approach to study multigenerational distillation, deriving exact recursion relations and the associated renormalization-group-like flows for two representative direct intergenerational distillation protocols at arbitrary teacher--student alignment strength. These flows reveal fixed-point structures, long-term dynamics, and critical behavior, yielding testable predictions for the critical transition between capability loss and stable transmission.

papers.title: ProLand: A New Infeasible Manifold Optimization Method for LoRA Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model-rank configuration.

papers.title: Agent-Controlled Forgetting for Tool-Using Agents: Reversible Context Curation in Practice
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents repeatedly carry observations whose useful content can be much smaller than their original payload. We study agent-controlled forgetting: the acting model selects previously observed tool results, replaces each with a short note at its original position, and retains the exact original in a recoverable archive. A Python harness exposes batch archival and explicit recovery without task-specific model training, while protecting user instructions and assistant messages from these operations. In an exploratory OpenTelemetry debugging case followed by an unrelated implementation task, the method ended with 231,951 provider-reported prompt tokens versus 912,492 under retained history, used 50% fewer cumulative input tokens, and had an estimated API cost of USD 1.28-1.44 versus approximately USD 4.38. Both arms passed the two-case primary behavioral oracle; neither fully satisfied the follow-up evaluation. The method made more requests and took 17% longer. A contrasting application-development pair produced no context or cost saving, and an earlier continuation exhibited lower manually assessed quality despite reduced context. These observations demonstrate substantial resource savings in noisy tool-use trajectories and identify workload dependence as a central consideration for reversible context management.

papers.title: CalibCause: A Quality-Gated, Interpretable and Calibrated Deep Learning Framework for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading
papers.abstract: Most deep learning systems for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are evaluated on a single data source, with limited evidence of cross-site generalisation, uncertainty calibration, and interpretability. We propose CalibCause, a quality-gated mixture-of-experts framework that combines per-expert visual explanations, label-free image-quality conditioning, knowledge distillation, and calibrated confidence with deferral. We evaluated the framework using 51,310 fundus images from EyePACS, DDR, and APTOS 2019, with IDRiD and DeepDRiD for external testing. Evaluation included pooled testing, leave-one-environment-out experiments, paired bootstrap confidence intervals, and local grade-threshold adaptation. On the pooled test split, the label-free distilled student achieved quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863 and accuracy of 0.865 with 27.8 million parameters, 52% fewer than its teacher. Across held-out environments, the label-free model achieved mean QWK of 0.741 compared with 0.743 for a plain ConvNeXt-Tiny baseline, while adversarial invariance did not improve cross-site grading accuracy. Refitting grade thresholds using 200 labelled images increased held-out EyePACS QWK from 0.533 to 0.621 for the label-free model. After vector scaling, expected calibration error ranged from 0.025 to 0.036 across CalibCause variants, and deferring the least confident 20% of images increased student accuracy from 0.865 to 0.923 on the remaining images. These findings demonstrate that quality-aware grading, interpretable expert routing, model compression, and calibrated deferral can be integrated without sacrificing cross-site performance relative to a plain baseline, although reliable deployment still requires local validation and adaptation.

papers.title: Darwin-Claw: Environment-Adaptive Experience Consolidation for Recursively Self-Evolving Agents
papers.abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. Furthermore, as foundational LLM reasoning improves, the bottleneck for agentic evolution shifts from accumulating generic knowledge to effectively managing situational experience. To address this, we propose Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive self-evolving framework that systematically distills episodic experiences to drive the comprehensive evolution of operational skills and durable memory. Theoretically grounded in an iterative agent-actor and evolver-critic co-adaptation, Darwin-Claw introduces a Hierarchical Experience Consolidation System that extracts fine-grained error attributions and generalizes them into dynamically updated prototype vectors. This structured situational experience serves as interaction patches for context-sensitive perception and explicit optimization signals for skill refinement. Practically, Darwin-Claw is a readily deployable, automated framework compatible with mainstream agent systems without requiring manual curation. Extensive experiments on WildClawBench demonstrate that Darwin-Claw yields substantial performance improvements, establishing a controllable and stable pathway for the continual, user-centric adaptation of autonomous agents in real-world ecosystems.

papers.title: Sensorium: An Open-Source Multimodal Data Collection and Curation Library for Embodied Surgical AI
papers.abstract: Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.

papers.title: Subspace Uncertainty and Sharp Sampling Thresholds on the Boolean Cube
papers.abstract: For a known finite-dimensional model subspace, classical Gaussian regression theory guarantees that least squares eventually attains the parametric rate, with prediction error scaling as the subspace dimension divided by the sample size. Yet subspaces with the same number of unknown coefficients can require very different sample sizes to reach this regime. For subspaces of polynomials on the Boolean cube, a fundamental question is how restrictions on degree and ambient dimension jointly determine this threshold. Our main result sharply characterizes the worst-subspace minimax sample threshold over a substantial parameter range, revealing an exponential dependence on degree and precisely quantifying the joint effects of degree, ambient dimension, and subspace dimension. A small modification of our lower-bound construction reveals a strong separation: a single subspace can admit noiseless recovery with optimal sample complexity independent of degree, yet require essentially the worst-case sample size, exponential in degree, to attain the noisy parametric rate. To establish the sampling lower bound, we sharpen the Polyanskiy-Samorodnitsky uncertainty principle (J. Funct. Anal., '19) to uniformly optimal precision and extend its concentration guarantee to large subspaces in which every function concentrates most of its energy on one shared Hamming ball. The sampling upper bound follows from the sharp moment bound of Kirshner and Samorodnitsky (IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory, '21) combined with empirical-process bounds.

papers.title: Safe Streaming Flow Planning by Aligning Sampling Dynamics with Execution Dynamics
papers.abstract: Generative planners based on diffusion/flow matching can learn to synthesize long-horizon trajectories from demonstrations. However, real-world deployment requires (i) enforcing safety constraints during execution and (ii) tight online replanning at fast execution rates. Prior safe diffusion/flow planners generate the agent's full trajectory at once, while repeatedly perturbing intermediate states to satisfy safety constraints. This approach is not only computationally intensive, but also introduces distribution shift since the learned sampling dynamics is distinct from the system's execution dynamics. We propose SafeStreamingFlow, a goal-conditioned planner that aligns flow sampling dynamics with execution dynamics by sequentially integrating a learned state vector field with hierarchical state prediction. Importantly, we need to enforce safety constraints only for the executed step via high order control barrier functions. Across navigation, racing, and locomotion benchmarks, SafeStreamingFlow reduces planning latency and improves safety compared to existing methods, while maintaining competitive goal-reaching success.

papers.title: Evaluating Jev on Arabic: Comparing Decision Models and LLMs Across Arabic Tasks and Dialects
papers.abstract: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.

papers.title: Post-Anomaly Detection Inference for Deep SVDD
papers.abstract: Deep Support Vector Data Description (Deep SVDD) has become a prominent framework for unsupervised anomaly detection by learning latent representations that compactly characterize normal data around a center. Despite its empirical success, anomaly decisions produced by Deep SVDD are typically made solely based on anomaly scores without rigorous statistical guarantees, thereby limiting their reliability in safety-critical and high-stakes applications where false positives must be strictly controlled. In this paper, we propose PADI (Post-Anomaly Detection Inference), a novel framework that equips a trained and frozen Deep SVDD detector with statistically valid inference by leveraging the Selective Inference framework. Specifically, PADI performs inference conditional on the event that a test instance is identified as anomalous by Deep SVDD, thereby enabling rigorous statistical assessment of anomaly decisions. Based on this formulation, we derive valid selective p-values that quantify the statistical significance of the detected anomaly. Using these p-values, we theoretically establish control of the false positive rate (FPR) at a user-specified significance level $α$ (e.g., $α=0.05$). Furthermore, we extend the proposed framework to Deep Semi-Supervised Anomaly Detection (Deep SAD), providing a principled approach for statistically reliable inference in semi-supervised anomaly detection settings. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets robustly support the theoretical findings. The results demonstrate that PADI consistently achieves proper FPR control while attaining superior true positive rates compared with existing approaches.

papers.title: ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research
papers.abstract: What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having 184 lead authors of 207 recent computer science papers label which candidates did or could have advanced their project, each with a detailed rationale. We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs.

papers.title: Geometry-Aided Channel Deduction with Partial Channel Estimates and Uncalibrated Digital Twin
papers.abstract: The acquisition of high-dimensional channel state information (CSI) in wireless MIMO-OFDM communications usually requires high pilot overhead, or relies on accurate and complete positional or environmental information. In this paper, we propose a geometry-aided channel deduction (GCD) approach, which utilizes an uncalibrated digital twin (DT) with only approximate environmental geometry and positions to assist the channel acquisition. The key rationale behind is that, even imprecise geometric information, which can be easily obtained in advance through radio sensing technologies or existing geographic databases, provides certain structural features about the current channel; meanwhile, the coarse instantaneous channel estimates using only a small amount of pilots provide dedicated information that aligns with the channel structure and further compensates for the geometry inaccuracy and other channel unknowns. To this end, we first extract geometric features from the DT, which contain only simple structural information of the channel. Then we propose random prompt augmentation, a novel method to generate an appropriate prompt that converts geometric multi-path structure into a CSI-like representation while suppressing the disturbance of other unknown channel parameters. The prompt is then fused with the pilot-based instantaneous channel estimate via a channel deduction network. To further enhance the network's versatility, we incorporate pilot configurations into the existing learning architecture to support variable pilot patterns. Comprehensive experiments validate the superiority of the proposed method, which demonstrates high channel acquisition quality, low pilot overhead, and strong robustness. Furthermore, the structural prompt also serves as scenario-related context, enabling our approach to generalize well in new scenarios.

papers.title: Physical Layer Anomaly Detection via Adaptive Gaussian Mixture Model
papers.abstract: Physical-layer spoofing attacks pose a critical threat to wireless localization systems by manipulating channel state information (CSI). Detecting such attacks becomes particularly challenging when the attacker and the legitimate node are spatially proximate, as their CSI characteristics become increasingly similar. To address this challenge in indoor scenarios, we propose an adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM)-based detection framework that learns legitimate CSI patterns and detects spatial inconsistency through statistical anomaly detection. Using a massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) experimental dataset with 64 uniform linear array (ULA) antenna and 5 mm spatial resolution, we evaluated our detector against CSI spoofing attacks with spatial displacements ranging from 50 mm to 450 mm. The adaptive GMM achieves 95-98% detection rate for displacements above 150 mm while maintaining 1% false alarm rate. We benchmark our approach against conventional GMM, local outlier factor (LOF), one-class support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) classifiers, demonstrating overall superior detection performance of our proposed classifier.

papers.title: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Spatiotemporal Brain MRI Forecasting
papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting of 3D anatomical changes is a critical generative vision challenge for modeling Alzheimer's Disease (AD) progression. While brain MRI forecasting from single-modality data has advanced, other key complementary multimodal biomarkers remain underutilized. In this work, we propose the Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Model (MC-LDM), a novel framework for patient-specific brain MRI synthesis. MC-LDM leverages multimodal biomarkers---MRI, tau-PET, Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), and APOE4---during training, but relies only on baseline MRI, APOE4, and patient metadata at inference, reflecting realistic clinical availability. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) fine-tuned via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for data-efficient learning; (2) a multimodal conditioning that integrates molecular and clinical signals to model heterogeneous disease trajectories; and (3) auxiliary predictors estimating unobserved multimodal biomarkers from MRI features and patient covariates to condition the diffusion model, removing the need for these assessments at inference. Trained on 1,355 visits from 852 subjects in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), MC-LDM reduces average regional volumetric MAE by 18% over the second-best baseline on an independent test set of 664 visits. To our knowledge, MC-LDM represents the first diffusion-based framework to leverage multimodal priors for MRI forecasting. This conceptual advancement enables patient-specific trajectory generation that captures aspects of AD heterogeneity not observable from structural anatomy alone, bridging the gap between rich multimodal supervision and the strict constraints of routine clinical deployment. Code is available at: https://github.com/antonioscardace/MC-LDM.

papers.title: Causal Localization of Evidence Effects in Transformers
papers.abstract: Can controlled symbolic inputs reveal attention heads that influence a language model's decisions from natural language evidence? We introduce controlled evidence aggregation (CEA), which varies the counts and order of two symbols in otherwise fixed prompts and measures changes in a frozen Transformer's preference between two answer tokens. The preference is measured by their logit difference; the prompts prescribe no correct answer. Balanced utility causal selection (BUC) identifies compact head sets by jointly evaluating how much ablating their outputs removes the count effect and how closely patching mean outputs between count conditions recovers the effect in both directions. We derive conditional bounds linking head attribution to intervention effects and specifying when the attribution shortlist can be recovered from finite samples. In Pythia-410M, ablating sets of 1-12 heads selected separately for four ordering regimes removes 65.5-91.6% of the count effect. The sets retain their influence on count comparisons not used for selection. To test relevance beyond symbolic inputs, we evaluate a natural language task asking which state is supported by more reports. Ablating eight heads selected only on symbolic yes/no prompts lowers mean accuracy by 8.2 percentage points, versus 0.8 for random sets matched by size and layer. Our results demonstrate that controlled symbolic probes can identify compact attention head sets whose causal influence extends to natural language decisions.

papers.title: Targeted Active Learning for Preference-Based Treatment Effects on Multivariate Outcomes
papers.abstract: Treatment efficacy is traditionally demonstrated on the basis of a single primary outcome. However, clinical decision-making usually requires consideration of multiple outcomes, balancing expected benefits against potential risks. The relative value assigned to these outcomes varies substantially from one patient to another. Given a preference rule over outcome profiles, treatment effects and optimal policies can be defined and estimated. Such a rule is rarely available in practice: it must itself be estimated from pairwise comparisons of outcome profiles, which are costly to collect from clinical experts. We propose an active learning framework that selects which comparisons to query. Standard criteria maximize the information gained on the preference rule itself. We instead target the quantities of interest, and select the query that most reduces uncertainty on the treatment effect and on the optimal policy induced by the learned rule. Under a Gaussian process model of the preference rule, we derive a closed-form approximation of this criterion. On semi-synthetic data built from a Parkinson's disease cohort with 13 clinical outcomes, our criterion achieves lower treatment effect estimation error and lower policy regret than existing criteria at equal query budget.

papers.title: Spectrally Targeted Muon
papers.abstract: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold $τ$, so that varying $τ$ interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix's isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

papers.title: Reliability of LLM Judges for Evaluating Entity Alignment
papers.abstract: Entity Alignment (EA) identifies equivalent entities across knowledge graphs and is critical for knowledge base integration and ontology merging. Evaluating EA systems at scale requires expensive expert annotation, making systematic assessment across diverse domains practically infeasible. LLM-as-judge evaluation offers a potentially scalable alternative, yet its reliability for structured prediction tasks like EA remains unstudied. We present the first systematic benchmarking study across three frontier models, three datasets, and four EA systems, using perturbation bias diagnostics, meta-evaluation across all dataset--judge--prompt combinations, and counterfactual label-flip tests. We identify anchor bias, a failure mode in which judges invert discrimination when the system's decision label is visible. Judge discrimination collapses under label-exposing prompts (J-ROC-AUC 0.12--0.87), while a label-free protocol recovers near-ceiling capability on distinctive-name datasets (0.98--1.00 for NeuSymEA) and significant recovery on biomedical pairs (0.93--0.95). Counterfactual label flips show that the visible label causally shifts scores by more than 2 points in 53--99% of pairs (FSR), with sensitivity growing with model capability, a pattern we call the frontier model paradox: stronger judges are more label-sensitive, not less, yet also better label-free predictors. The direction of the shifts is mixed, so we report this as an observed pattern. A blinded two-annotator human evaluation (102 pairs, Cohen's $κ$ = 0.902) provides a gold-label reference. We release the first biomedical EA benchmark (MeSH--SNOMED CT, 15K pairs) and a reproducible auditing framework for LLM judge reliability in EA. Code and data are available at https://github.com/vaibhavalakshmiravideshik/llm-as-a-judge-entity-alignment.

papers.title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information
papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate $R^\star$ as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset--receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone.
