papers.title: Anytime Contracts for AI Services
papers.abstract: AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.

papers.title: Cyber-physical attack detection approaches in the wide-area measurement system
papers.abstract: Improving situational awareness within the Smart Grid is an effective preventive measure to detect potential anomalies, and avoid their adverse consequences. A wide area measurement system (WAMS) based Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) can assist in improving visibility within the grid by collecting relevant measurements including magnitude, phase angle, frequency, voltage, and current, with a precise GPS-based timestamp. So far, there are more than 2500 PMUs deployed in the North American power grid, where each of which generates between 30 and 60 samples/s, roughly 1.5 TB/month of streamed data. Thus, processing such large PMU streams requires expensive computational resources and faster algorithms. This paper provides state-of-the-art cyber and physical anomalies in the WAMS and analyses their impact on the integrity and availability of the system. Next, it investigates the current anomaly detection approach in historical and streaming PMU data, including conventional machine learning and hybrid approaches, and assesses their advantages and main drawbacks. Lastly, it sheds light on the importance of handling missing PMU data and concept drifts.

papers.title: Soft Teacher Forcing
papers.abstract: Soft tokens have so far been used to replace discrete chain-of-thought in latent reasoning methods. These approaches typically require multi-stage training and, in some cases, auxiliary modules, yet they still underperform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on <input, chain-of-thought, output> triples. In this paper, we ask whether soft tokens can be used to improve SFT itself, instead of as an avenue for latent reasoning. We introduce Soft Teacher Forcing (Soft-TF), a simple training algorithm that combines teacher-forced embeddings with soft tokens through random convex combinations. The soft tokens are computed in a single parallel forward pass over the ground-truth sequence. Soft-TF adds no parameters, no external model and no curriculum, and leaves inference unchanged. Experiments show that Soft-TF improves over SFT on GSM8K, MATH, MathQA and AQuA, by +2.1 to +4.1 points on GSM8K across seven Gemma, Llama and Mistral models.

papers.title: SPIRIT: Sparse Physics-Informed Inverse Rendering for SAR Imaging
papers.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) and wave-based imaging systems play a critical role in sensing under adverse conditions, but are fundamentally constrained by a trade-off between collection speed and spatial resolution. Reducing measurements to enable rapid collection of fragment geometric information across sensing dimensions, leading to highly non-injective inverse problems that destabilize conventional image-domain reconstruction and super-resolution methods. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) exemplifies this challenge in sparse-aperture sampling. We introduce SPIRIT, a physics-informed inverse rendering framework for sparse-aperture SAR. Rather than enhancing formed images, SPIRIT reconstructs an explicit three-dimensional surface. By adopting an optimization strategy and explicitly modeling visibility, phase coherence, and wave propagation, SPIRIT aggregates distributed geometric features across sparse aperture views into a coherent reconstruction. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that SPIRIT recovers accurate geometry and signal under extreme sparsity, reducing data collection by over 90% while achieving low geometric and signal error and consistently outperforming baselines.

papers.title: Small Language Models for Smart Data Model Classification at the Edge: A Cost-Aware Hybrid Approach
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous data sources within the Internet of Things (IoT) across domains such as smart cities, energy management, and environmental monitoring necessitates efficient and scalable data standardization methods. Effective classification of smart data models (SDMs) is essential for facilitating interoperability. However, existing approaches are often limited by high resource consumption and lack applicability in edge environments with constrained computational capabilities. Aiming to bridge this gap, the proposed study evaluates the performance of lightweight open-source language models (LMs) to resolve an input data entity against its corresponding best fitting SDM representation under resource-constrained conditions. It systematically benchmarks a diverse array of models, including general purpose (GP), reasoning-specialized (RS), and code-specialized (CS) architectures, across multiple domain-specific datasets. Addressing the current omission of lightweight, resource-efficient solutions in the literature, the investigation provides significant and valuable insights into model selection, task formulation, and deployment strategies that optimize accuracy and efficiency. A complementary experiment also compares the surveyed large language models (LLMs) against two near-zero-cost similarity baselines (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and a lightweight sentence encoder) on the same task, providing a strong reference point for interpreting the practical value of LLM-based classification on edge platforms.

papers.title: ChronoCulture: Evaluating Cultural Awareness Across Time in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Cultural attitudes and social norms evolve over time, yet most cultural benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) treat culture as a static attribute of a country or region. We introduce ChronoCulture, a benchmark of 10,360 temporal pairs built from longitudinal survey data across 72 countries. Each pair contains the same survey question asked in the same country in an older and a newer year, with full population response distributions as ground truth. Across six LLMs, we find that models can often predict a country's attitudes at one point in time but do not reliably capture how those attitudes change. Their predictions for different years tend to stay close together, failing to capture much of the observed change. Specifying the intended year in the prompt also offers little overall improvement in alignment with survey responses. These findings suggest that models often present a largely static picture of cultural attitudes, highlighting the need to evaluate cultural awareness across time.

papers.title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training
papers.abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.

papers.title: Action Transfer Across Character Body Plans in Latent-Action World Models: An Empirical Study of Animated Characters
papers.abstract: Latent-action world models learn actions from video without labels, and recent methods aim to share these actions across bodies. Transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored. In this paper, we study whether an action learned from one character can make a character with a different body perform the same action. A cat, a blob and a human can all jump, but each moves its body in its own way. The usual transfer gain mixes body motion with screen movement and can assign a perfect score to a model that ignores its action. To address this, we introduce a transfer score that compares the correct action with wrong ones from the same source. We test five training objectives on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D. With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models. In contrast, with a camera that follows the body, the best model reaches only 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans. With this camera, a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%). The learned actions therefore retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character.

papers.title: Mitigating Popularity Bias in Recommendation with Global Listwise Learning and Progressive Bi-Weighting
papers.abstract: In recommender systems, user feedback typically follows a long-tail distribution, which leads many recommendation algorithms to exacerbate popularity bias by disproportionately favoring popular items. To mitigate this issue, recent studies have employed Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) to rebalance training data via reweighting user-item interactions. However, the effectiveness of IPS-based approaches is often constrained by locally unbiased objectives and inaccurate propensity estimation. In this paper, we propose Multinomial Likelihood with Bi-Weighting (Mult-BiW) to address these limitations. First, we introduce a debiasing framework, termed Mult-IPS, which integrates multinomial likelihood with IPS to capture global and unbiased user preferences over the entire item set. Second, we develop a Bi-Weighting (BiW) strategy that jointly leverages propensity scores and a collection model, incorporating a smoothing mechanism to enhance the robustness of propensity estimation. We further provide theoretical analyses that establish an upper bound on the empirical bias and characterize the optimal form of the collection model. Third, to mitigate the adverse effects of aggressive reweighting on representation learning, we design a Progressive Bi-Weighting strategy that gradually transitions from discriminative representation learning to popularity debiasing. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that Mult-BiW consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Severity-Channel Conditioning: An Injection-Level Study for Consumer-Device Deblurring
papers.abstract: Motion-deblurring models lose substantial accuracy when transferred from professional cameras to smartphone-derived imagery. This paper studies whether a severity descriptor, partly derived from the paired sharp target, helps adaptation on the iPhoneBlur consumer-device benchmark. Under a shared update budget, input concatenation of a severity map is compared with global feature modulation by capture metadata, spatial feature modulation by the severity map, and a tier-contrastive output objective, together with an unconditioned spectral-loss control, all fine-tuned from the same domain-adapted latent-diffusion baseline. The primary experiment is an oracle diagnostic: target-derived information is supplied at inference. For the evaluated model pair, input concatenation improves overall peak signal-to-noise ratio from 31.23 to 31.30 dB, whereas feature modulation, the contrastive objective, and the spectral-loss control do not exceed the baseline. The gain is positive on 87.2% of test images and on 14 of 15 held-out source videos; this video-level analysis describes the evaluated checkpoint pair and does not establish robustness to retraining, and three training seeds are reported separately. The input-level gain recurs on a transformer backbone. In one exploratory run, zeroing the channel at inference retains most of the gain in peak signal-to-noise ratio but lowers structural similarity below the baseline. A normalized-step diagnostic does not support the expected larger-gradient explanation. The results characterize the evaluated configurations and do not establish injection location as the sole cause, a spatial-locality mechanism, or a reliable deployment advantage.

papers.title: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
papers.abstract: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.

papers.title: FuzzInsight: Navigating the Efficiency-Effectiveness Trade-off in Coverage-Guided DNN Fuzzing
papers.abstract: Collecting and labeling diverse test datasets for evaluating Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is costly and time-consuming. This has motivated coverage-guided fuzzing techniques that generate defect-revealing corner cases from limited test data. However, their effectiveness depends heavily on configuration choices, particularly coverage criteria and seed-selection strategies. We present a configuration-oriented analysis and decision guidelines for scalable DNN fuzzing targeting two bottlenecks: inefficient seed utilization and the cost of coverage guidance. Our analysis shows that existing seed-selection strategies repeatedly prioritize a small subset of inputs, leaving many collected seeds unexplored. To address this issue, we propose Equalized Sampling, a constraint-based strategy that increases mean seed queue utilization to 77%, improving on prior approaches by 13 percentage points. We further evaluate 84 fuzzing configurations on four benchmark datasets: MNIST, SVHN, GTSRB, and CIFAR-100. Results show that the non-structural criteria LSCD, LSC, and MDSC achieve coverage outcomes comparable to structural and alternative non-structural criteria while requiring substantially less computation. These criteria also promote broad behavioral exploration of the DNN under test, reducing the need to monitor multiple coverage metrics. Among them, LSCD provides a modest but consistent runtime advantage. Finally, we show that retraining with generated corner cases improves generalization robustness by up to 77 percentage points on average without degrading performance on the original test distribution. Together, these findings provide a practical blueprint for selecting fuzzing configurations that balance efficiency, behavioral exploration, and model hardening.

papers.title: MIPS: Mitigating Mode Collapse in Reinforcement Learning for Large Outcome Spaces
papers.abstract: Expected-reward maximization in reinforcement learning concentrates probability mass on a few outcomes, even in tasks that require many distinct, high-quality solutions, a failure known as mode collapse. Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) counters this in group-based policy gradients such as GRPO by dividing each reward by the outcome's probability, estimated from its frequency within the sampled group. When the outcome space is large relative to the group, outcomes rarely repeat and these estimates become uninformative. Since an outcome can be constructed along many trajectories, its probability is a sum over all of them, and computing it directly is intractable. We propose Marginal IPS (MIPS), which performs marginal evaluation by combining the sampled trajectory with a learned model of the trajectories that lead to each outcome. On Hypergrids, where the exact sampling distribution is computable, MIPS stays near the reward-distribution target as the outcome space grows relative to the rollout group, while frequency-based IPS degrades. In molecular synthesis and phylogenetic inference, MIPS sustains diverse, high-quality sampling where GRPO and frequency-based IPS collapse, showing that MIPS serves as a reliable solution to mode collapse in RL.

papers.title: An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells
papers.abstract: Understanding the persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety motivates an investigation of the dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry studied in singular learning theory. We analyze this persistence through transitions between singular wells. We establish an Eyring-Kramers formula for a low temperature Langevin diffusion between two compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. The wells may be singular and nonisolated, and the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle, with gates understood as inclusion-minimal sets meeting every minimizing path. A boundary-gate construction shows that uniqueness of this inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to every minimizing path passing through the saddle and one such path meeting the communication level only there. Compact semianalytic topology provides a separating function away from a fixed saddle neighborhood; analytic Morse coordinates give matching capacity bounds by first sending the temperature to zero and then shrinking that neighborhood. An anchored energy estimate and a small-ball potential-theoretic identity give uniformity for deterministic starting points. The leading constant is expressed in terms of the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor, and the saddle Hessian.

papers.title: RoboAuto: Autonomous Robot Program Search through Multi-Level Physical Understanding
papers.abstract: Recently, LLM-based autonomous agents have shown strong capabilities in iteratively generating, evaluating, and refining executable solutions. In robotic manipulation, Code-as-Policy lets these agents search over modular and editable robot programs. However, effective program search requires physical understanding: agents must understand how objects can be manipulated, how scene geometry constrains actions, and why interactions succeed or fail. Existing methods rely mainly on execution feedback for program refinement, often leaving these physical questions unresolved. We introduce RoboAuto, a framework for robot program search that explicitly organizes physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels through three components. First, a hierarchical knowledge base combines executable skills with object-centric knowledge of affordances, spatial relations, and action effects, learned from embodied data and online task solving. Second, scene grounding connects this knowledge to the current environment by identifying relevant objects and resolving action-critical quantities. Third, multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments checks whether each stage produces its expected physical effects and actively tests competing hypotheses to resolve physical uncertainties. RoboAuto achieves superior performance across five benchmark families, attaining an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than twice the mean success rate of ASPIRE on LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus. It also outperforms ASPIRE and $π_{0.5}$ on three challenging long-horizon real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation. We further show that the knowledge base transfers across simulators and embodiments, and that program search performance scales with its size. Project page: https://roboauto-ai.github.io/

papers.title: Confessions of a Masked MDP
papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning, one presumes the action set to be known ahead of time, and, thus, one must know if any state-action pairs are not permissible ahead of computations. In some applications, determining this action mask is the main computational bottleneck. Isolating this problem to highlight its core properties, we study how to combine the search for an optimal policy with the learning of the mask itself, under a linear MDP model in which each attempted action reveals the exact value of a linear score determining its validity. In this framework, we first construct an algorithm based on deterministic optimistic optimization and show that it is minimax optimal, which we show is also computationally efficient. However, it is sub-optimal on non-degenerate instances, as we show. We propose an alternative, which is also computationally efficient, which plans its exploration strategy. This algorithm admits a formal interpretation as an analogue of information-directed-sampling for deterministic feedback, which may be of independent interest. Finally, we study an application of this framework to transfer learning, where the invalid action set changes over time.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Crowd Flow Control Using Dynamic Barriers
papers.abstract: Crowd barriers are widely used to regulate pedestrian movement during large public events such as pilgrimages. However, fixed barrier layouts often create unnecessary stopping and local congestion even when they successfully control the overall crowd flow. Finding better barrier configurations is difficult because there is no dataset that provides the best barrier placement for a given crowd scene. We address this challenge by introducing a simulation-driven reinforcement learning framework that learns barrier configurations without requiring labelled training data. Starting from a segmented crowd scene, we construct a realistic simulation environment that reproduces the observed pedestrian distribution. This environment is then used to train a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agent that continuously adjusts barrier positions to improve pedestrian movement. Unlike supervised approaches the proposed framework allows the agent to explore barrier configurations that have never been observed in real data. We evaluate the learned policy under unseen numbers of pedestrians. The learned policy consistently outperforms the existing manually designed barrier configuration by reducing pedestrian stops while maintaining effective flow regulation. These results demonstrate that combining computer vision crowd simulation and reinforcement learning provides an effective framework for optimizing crowd control infrastructure.

papers.title: Algorithmic Monoculture in Machine Learning-based Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendation
papers.abstract: Machine learning recommendations are often evaluated one model at a time, despite deployment across interconnected decision makers. For continuous NPK fertilizer prescriptions, correlated errors can aggregate across farms and generate systemic costs. A model of shared and farm-specific recommendation errors links expected social loss to model adoption shares; the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index characterizes concentration effects when common model errors are independent and predictive risks are equal. A covariance-generalized formulation captures the dependence between model families. A two-model threshold characterizes when privately optimal monoculture is socially dominated, and a convex portfolio rule limits average private predictive regret. Nine model families across five Moroccan cereal systems provide a benchmark-based calibration. Under illustrative parameters and a 10% regret cap, accuracy-constrained diversification lowers modeled social loss in all five systems by 10.89-41.53% (mean 19.41%). Uniform allocation reduces modeled loss in this setting, but breaches the regret cap in every crop. Correlation sensitivity shows that highly dependent model errors attenuate the benefits of diversification. These counterfactual outcomes are not estimates of agronomic or monetary welfare; the framework identifies adoption architecture and error dependence as ecosystem-level evaluation variables.

papers.title: Constraint-Preserving Flow Matching for Spectral Graph Generation
papers.abstract: Spectral graph generation models graphs through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of their Laplacians, providing a compact and continuous alternative to direct graph construction. However, these eigensystems must retain the structural properties of graph Laplacians. Existing approaches preserve eigenvector orthonormality but do not enforce the Laplacian nullspace constraint, potentially producing eigensystems inconsistent with Laplacian structure. To address this, we introduce Laplacian-Constrained Stiefel Flow Matching (LaSFM), which preserves the nullspace condition alongside eigenvector orthonormality and positive eigenvalues during generation. We characterize the underlying constrained Stiefel manifold and formulate flow matching on it. We further extend LaSFM to property-guided generation, steering samples toward desired graph properties while maintaining these constraints. Experiments demonstrate improved performance on both spectral and graph-level metrics, along with better alignment with target properties.

papers.title: Beyond Owls: Subliminal Learning Can Transfer Learned Capabilities and Backdoors
papers.abstract: In subliminal learning (SL), a teacher model passes on a trait to a student model by distillation on data semantically unrelated to the trait. So far, SL has been demonstrated for only a limited range of traits, including preferences for animals (e.g., owls) and malicious personas. These traits can also be elicited with simple prompts or with steering. Can SL transfer a wider range of traits, including more complex ones? If so, distillation might transfer subtle forms of misalignment (e.g., reward-seeking, scheming, and secret loyalties) without detection. To this end, we test whether SL can transfer a novel capability: predicting the outputs of a randomly initialized MLP. After distilling on unrelated text, the student achieves substantial performance on the task, while falling short of the teacher. We find that a directly optimized steering vector matches SL in distribution but generalizes worse out of distribution. Next, we test whether SL can transfer backdoors. We finetune the teacher to answer in French when the prompt contains a female name, then distill on number sequences containing neither names nor French. The student partially acquires the backdoor, responding in French on 23.5% of prompts with female names versus 0.0% with male names. Finally, we test whether SL can transfer a propensity to hack in an agentic chess environment. We finetune the student on number sequences from a steered hacker teacher. The student hacks in 58.3% of episodes, compared with 10.9% for the unfinetuned model. Thus, we show SL can transfer capabilities, backdoors, and hacking propensities. The amount of transfer is sensitive to the setup. In several experiments, it is made stronger by using logit distillation or by restricting LoRA to the attention layers.

papers.title: Global Communication or Graph-Specific Memory?
papers.abstract: Scalable Graph Transformers are commonly trained and evaluated on static large graphs in a transductive setup. Many scalable Graph Transformer components can be formulated as a constant-size shared memory, similar to virtual nodes, providing compressed information about the whole graph. The counterpart of these models in language models and other domains is justified as the input changes, and this mechanism learns to compress some useful information about the input. In transductive learning on a single fixed graph, however, any shared memory can be seen as a constant at test time. This raises the question of what exactly this shared memory does in this static setup. We give preliminary evidence that optimizing a shared memory directly performs similarly to global communication methods, and so normal local message-passing models can embed similar information in their weights. Thus, these settings may be a poor fit for evaluating global communication in graph neural networks.

papers.title: Which Language Should a Skeleton Speak? Language Choices in Multilingual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Skeleton-based reasoning prompting is a promising training-free approach for structuring LLM reasoning, but prior work largely assumes an English-centric setting. We propose the Language-Aware Skeleton Exploration Framework (LASEF) to study skeleton-language choice in multilingual mathematical reasoning. Across math benchmarks, model scales, and languages, we show that English skeletons yield a small positive tendency on average, most visible for smaller models and low-resource languages. However, few language-level gains remain significant after correction, and English is not universally optimal. Combining greedy decoding, multi-rollout evaluation, translation ablation, and cross-benchmark validation, we further find three patterns of skeleton-language effects: directionally consistent, evaluation- and benchmark-dependent, and asymmetric negative. These effects cannot be fully explained by generation quality alone. Overall, skeleton language is a context-dependent design variable that requires multi-level exploration. All resources are released at https://github.com/lhsstn/LASEF.

papers.title: Beyond CLIP: Calibrated (Few-Shot) Defect Detection With System One Decision Models
papers.abstract: Cameras and vision sensors are widely used for product and process inspection in manufacturing environments. Traditionally, this process required thousands of images of both nominal and defective products to train such models. Recent research shows that vision transformer (ViT) models, such as CLIP, can reduce this requirement to 50-100 images per nominal and defective class. However, collecting even 50 defective images can be difficult in high-yield or low-volume manufacturing processes. In this paper, we examine the utility of two recently proposed structured decision models (Jev and Clef-Flash) in applications using as few as k=2 reference images per class at inference. In the process, we provide three main contributions: (a) a framework for k-shot learning of these models for image classification/inspection applications; (b) an agentic approach for automatically refining the text descriptions that guide image classification in these decision models; and (c) an approach to calibrate the resulting defect probabilities to improve their reliability for inspection decisions. We test these contributions in five manufacturing case studies. Using two reference images per class, both Jev and Clef-Flash outperform CLIP's test accuracies with the same references (0.75-1.00 [Jev] and 0.71-0.99 [Clef-Flash] vs 0.67-0.84 [CLIP]). Furthermore, we show that our agentic refinement of text descriptions significantly improves accuracy across 6 of 8 model-application combinations, and our calibration approach reduces the Brier score in 13 of the 15 model-application configurations. To support the reproducibility of our work, we provide our replication code and have created the R "decisions" package for evaluating additional models. We also provide a publicly available web app that allows practitioners to inspect their own images with no code.

papers.title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
papers.abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.

papers.title: DraftTrace: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing
papers.abstract: Generative AI has changed how students produce writing assignments. The final artifact is no longer sufficient to understand the process through which it was produced. We introduce DraftTrace, a writing environment that jointly captures three complementary views of writing: the final product, the writing process and interactions with an integrated AI-assistant. DraftTrace reconstructs how a document develops over time and organizes these signals into submission, longitudinal, and class-level analytics for instructors. We deployed DraftTrace in a graduate NLP course with 81 students and compared their sessions with LLM-generated responses entered by automated tools and with copy-typed responses. While product measures distinguish differences in text formulation, process measures distinguish differences in how text is entered. Considering both views together helps characterize cases such as copy-typing. Interaction traces show that students use the assistant differently across stages of writing: to clarify the question at an early stage and to verify answers at a later stage. A preliminary instructor survey highlights the importance of multi-view writing analytics and their interpretability.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Visual Agent via Margin Reward
papers.abstract: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks. However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images. Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver's capabilities. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver's performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1\% --- demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision.

papers.title: Conformal Risk Certificates for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty: A Gated Reinforcement-Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning portfolio policies can optimize allocations from prices, covariances, and prior positions, yet they lack a calibrated, replayable mechanism for certifying that a proposed allocation respects a bounded risk envelope before execution. Regulators increasingly expect automated portfolio systems to provide exactly this kind of pre-trade audit trail, interpretable risk limit, and human-oversight mechanism. Gated Conformal Semantic Risk Control addresses this gap by separating return-seeking allocation from text-conditioned downside-risk verification. An instruction-tuned language model maps timestamped disclosures into schema-validated semantic risk states over macro, liquidity, earnings, and sector channels. These states induce correlated ellipsoidal factor-shock uncertainty sets whose conformal radii are calibrated by rolling finite-sample prediction over localized semantic nonconformity buckets. An asymmetric second-order cone gate then checks each raw PPO proposal against a certified worst-case semantic loss budget. The gate stays inactive for compliant proposals and intervenes only when that budget is exceeded. In walk-forward out-of-sample tests on nine liquid U.S. Select Sector SPDR ETFs, Raw PPO earns a 12.7% annual return while incurring a 4.05% semantic violation rate. Gated-CSRC removes all observed out-of-sample semantic limit breaches while retaining an 11.7% annual return. This 100-basis-point auditable safety premium is smaller than the yield loss imposed by unconditional hard projection, and exact McNemar testing confirms the compliance gain at $p < 10^{-15}$. Loughran-McDonald lexicon controls and time-shuffled text controls fail to reproduce this certificate.

papers.title: Do the Details Help the Whole? One-Way Transfer from Person Actions to Group Intent in VLMs on JRDB-Social
papers.abstract: Social scene datasets label people at two levels: what each person is doing and what the group is there for. Training on both levels at once is often assumed to help each of them. We test this assumption for vision-language models (VLMs) on JRDB-Social, treating person actions as the details and group intent as the whole. We fine-tune Qwen3.5 4B under eight training arms with three seeds, repeat the core arms on Qwen3.5 9B and Qwen3-VL 4B, and judge every arm with a verdict rule fixed before testing. Writing each member's actions before the intent raises intent macro-F1 from 30.1 to 31.0, and writing the intent first reaches 31.2, while action F1 stays within 0.2 points of an action-only model. Under the selected recipe, no arm trained with intent improves actions. The gain requires correct, image-grounded actions: empty action lists or actions borrowed from another group with the same intent lower intent F1. Forced-prefix tests, occlusion, member masking, linear probes and component grafting show that the intent follows the written actions, relies more on people and partly resides in the vision tower. Supplying actions as input instead of as targets hurts both levels.

papers.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
papers.abstract: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.

papers.title: MoF: Preference-Aware Mixture Modeling for Black-Box LLM Personalization
papers.abstract: Proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks, yet aligning their outputs with diverse user preferences remains challenging. Existing personalization approaches for black-box LLMs often rely on user-specific scoring heads, causing the number of personalized parameters to grow linearly with the number of users and requiring additional adaptation for unseen users. To address these limitations, we propose Mixture-of-Facets (MoF), a scalable personalization framework for black-box LLMs that models user preferences as compositions of shared latent preference facets rather than dedicated user-specific parameters. MoF performs personalization through history-conditioned routing over shared facet heads, enabling personalization for users unseen during training without additional parameter updates. Across diverse personalization tasks, MoF delivers stronger personalization performance while maintaining a more scalable and parameter-efficient design than prior approaches. Additional analysis indicates strong generalization to unseen users.

papers.title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points
papers.abstract: Every recurrence of a looped language model adds cost in training, decoding, prefill, and reinforcement learning (RL). The closer recurrent states get to fixed points, the less the path to them matters. This enables truncated backpropagation in training; terminal key-value (KV) sharing for decoding with almost no loss in accuracy; a distilled student that prefills up to 1.79x faster; and RL updates that compute gradients from saved rollout states, 2x faster than backpropagating through the replayed trajectory. We therefore improve the two components of training that shape these fixed points: the depth prior and input injection. Fixed-depth training breaks KV sharing, and Huginn's broad depth prior supports sharing but dilutes supervision at the target depth more than sharing requires; we learn the prior from prediction feedback, with an entropy term that keeps it broad. Existing injection schemes let the state's component along the input amplify or cancel the injection; we remove this component with orthogonal injection. From 100M to 1.6B parameters, the learned prior and orthogonal injection lower perplexity at every scale relative to Huginn's prior and existing injection schemes, respectively. At 1.6B, the learned prior with a 3x smaller KV cache matches the downstream average of fixed-depth training with the full cache.

papers.title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification
papers.abstract: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We compare a deterministic U-Net with conditional flow matching (Flow), conditional diffusion (EDM), and a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge (VP-DDBM) for two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, each model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. At two thermal gradients outside the training range, we compare surrogate rollouts spanning \(48{,}000\) phase-field Euler steps with five phase-field futures generated from a common restart at each gradient. With two network evaluations per transition, Flow achieves the lowest time-averaged fair continuous ranked probability score among the generative surrogates for mean phase, mean Cu concentration, interface length, and leading-tip position at both gradients. Flow also reproduces the cellular morphology and retains sharp solid--liquid interfaces. It generates a single future approximately \(107\times\) faster than the phase-field solver on the reported hardware, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.

papers.title: MSC: Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control Framework with Uncertainty-Aware NMPC and RL-based Execution Layer
papers.abstract: Freely swiveling casters are widely adopted in industrial AMRs/SDVs for their mechanical simplicity and load capacity. However, caster misalignment during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers induces strong contact nonlinearities, widening the planning-execution gap between commanded $(v, ω)$ and realized motion. Existing caster-aware strategies are highly sensitive to state-estimation reliability, causing unstable execution in uncertain transition regimes. To address this, we present Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control (MSC), a planning-execution integrated hierarchical framework featuring two core mechanisms. First, an uncertainty-aware NMPC (CU-MPC) dynamically schedules caster-aware costs and input regularization using predictive uncertainty to suppress overly aggressive maneuvers. Second, a reinforcement learning-based execution layer estimates and predicts caster states under partial observability, transforming high-level velocity commands into physically executable wheel speeds adapted to current contact conditions. Validations in Isaac Sim and real robots demonstrate that MSC offers a clear comparative advantage over existing decoupled compensation approaches by significantly improving caster-state estimation accuracy, minimizing misalignment, and enhancing tracking robustness in caster-sensitive maneuvers.

papers.title: From Retrieval to Customer Context: Evaluating Frontier-Model Systems for Voice-of-Customer Analysis
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly use frontier language models to analyze customer feedback, but answer quality also depends on how that feedback is organized and made available. We define a \emph{customer context graph} as a unified model of customer and business context. Typed relationships connect customer objects (feedback, conversations, users, and accounts), operational objects (tickets, support agents, opportunities, and competitors), and analytical or action objects (taxonomy concepts, evidence, insights, work items, and outcomes). This lets an agent investigate not only what customers say, but why, who is affected, what action followed, who owns it, and whether it was resolved. For this experiment, the graph is populated from public Cursor feedback; the same architecture can support any type of feedback source. We compare Agentic RAG, a Deep Research Agent, and a Customer Context Graph-backed Agent on the same 9,432 public Cursor feedback records using 30 realistic product, incident, comparison, and metadata questions. Without exhaustive ground truth, we jointly score responses on answer quality (coverage and organization), analytical depth (specificity and decomposition), and evidence quality (citation support and traceability), using a comparative rubric calibrated on 28 of the 30 questions. We sample cited records against their claims and weight the three dimensions equally. Under this aligned rubric, the Customer Context Graph-backed Agent scores 0.961 overall, versus 0.710 for the Deep Research Agent and 0.651 for Agentic RAG, and leads the Deep Research Agent on 27 of 30 paired questions (sign-test p < 10^(-5); strictly best on 26 of 30). Its largest advantage is analytical depth (0.967 versus 0.642), reflecting more specific, hierarchically developed findings with quantified themes and traceable evidence...

papers.title: Retrieval-Centric Deep Learning in Growing Nonparametric Neural Networks
papers.abstract: We investigate a general-purpose layer for deep learning that, instead of compressing arbitrary-size training data into fixed-size weight matrices, stores a new pair of key-value representations for every data point during training, and retrieves and recombines these representations through an attention mechanism at inference time - resulting in a growing neural net (NN). While Irie et al. (arXiv:2202.05798) have put forward this perspective from the classic duality expressing any linear layer in a deep NN trained by gradient descent as linear attention (LA) over the training data points, replacing LA by more powerful attention functions, as they suggest, turns out to be non-trivial: we show that naively applying learning rules from the LA case to advanced kernels does not lead to principled optimization. Here we fill this gap and develop functional gradient-based learning rules for kernelized attention layers, based on radial basis function (RBF) and softmax-like kernels - establishing the principled "retrieval-centric deep learning" (RCDL) paradigm. Empirically, we demonstrate the promising performance and learning-efficiency of RCDL on image classification and synthetic teacher-student learning tasks. Moreover, we show that replacing LA in the dual form of NNs by advanced LA variants, namely MesaNet/DeltaNet, yields a formal connection to recently proposed optimizers for conventional fixed-size NNs, offering a novel perspective on deep learning optimization.

papers.title: How to scale your HEP ML models: A recipe for robust architecture comparisons at scale
papers.abstract: Much of the recent progress in machine learning domains such as language models has come from scaling laws that predict performance as a function of training effort. In high-energy physics (HEP) similar behavior has now been observed. To aid further study, we present a systematic procedure to derive robust scaling laws and compare design choices on the relevant budget axes for HEP tasks. We first validate the full scaling trajectory on toy problems and then apply the procedure to multi-task transformers on the ~11 billion-jet ATLAS JetSet2 dataset, in both the compute- and data-constrained regimes. For the latter, we predict, to the best of our knowledge for the first time, the jointly optimal model size, training horizon, learning rate and batch size under early stopping. At compute-optimal scaling, we recover a near-equal $\sqrt{C}$ dependence of model and dataset size, and find that auxiliary objectives lower the primary jet-classification loss at equal compute budget. Expanding the inputs toward lower-level data systematically lowers the loss while leaving the scaling exponent nearly unchanged. The onset of the power-law regime is itself set by scale: below a threshold in dataset size the loss carries little information about high-compute scaling, underscoring the value of large, high-quality full-simulation datasets as a foundation for scaling studies and the development of foundation models in HEP.

papers.title: OmniCam: Omni-Camera Trajectory Generation via Geometry-Grounded Pose Token Learning
papers.abstract: Camera trajectories control viewpoint changes in video generation, scene reconstruction, and robotic perception. Generating them from language requires both scene geometry and target-aware framing. We introduce OmniCam, an autoregressive model that generates camera pose sequences from a single panorama and textual trajectory descriptions. Its geometry-grounded pose token learning combines three components: a panoramic point-cloud encoder for omnidirectional geometric context; hybrid absolute-rotation and relative-translation tokenization with temporally consistent quaternion signs; and separate geometric and semantic conditioning streams with an explicit 3D target anchor. We also construct OmniCaT, containing 267,700 trajectories across four camera behaviors. On the reported OmniCaT evaluation, OmniCam reduces trajectory errors by 28--47% and collision rate by 65.8% relative to GenDoP retrained on OmniCaT. Against the best baseline for each metric, the ATE and collision reductions are 43.0% and 62.3%, respectively. Component ablations support the use of geometric and target-aware conditioning, while downstream experiments examine camera-controlled video generation and robotic active perception.

papers.title: Rubric Curriculum RL: Exploiting the Generation-Verification Gap in Non-Verifiable Domains
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has led to significant gains in math and code generation. Extending these gains to open-ended domains remains challenging: ground-truth verification is unavailable, human annotation is expensive, and learned reward models are prone to reward hacking. The generation-verification gap, where judging good outputs is easier than producing them, offers a potential path to improvement. However, rubric-based judges are often imprecise and stationary, so policies can overfit or reward hack them. We introduce Rubric Curriculum RL (RcRL), which exploits this gap without new data, human annotations, or stronger teacher models. We combine pairwise preferences over rollouts with a curriculum over rubric criteria, yielding a more discriminative signal than absolute scoring and a non-stationary objective. Whereas baselines plateau within a few hundred steps, RcRL preserves output entropy and keeps improving past 1000 steps. On creative writing, RcRL achieves a 70.5% human win rate against the base model, with gains across benchmarks and judges. On HealthBench, RcRL improves over the base model by 14.6% (full set) and 25.4% (consensus subset), outperforming all training baselines, including instance-specific rubrics.

papers.title: Integrating multi-source local information for global undirected graph reconstruction via integer programming
papers.abstract: Graphical models are widely used to represent conditional independence structures, but learning them is challenging when data are fragmented across sources that measure different subsets of variables and may not be directly shareable. We develop a general framework for reconstructing a shared global graph from heterogeneous, partially observed sources. Our framework permits both the observed variable sets and source-specific distributions to differ. Under a source-wise faithfulness condition, local conditional independence graphs correspond to latent projections of the shared global graph, which is identifiable up to the equivalence class induced by the observed variable sets. The framework integrates raw data, estimated source graphs, or a combination of both, accommodating settings with restricted access to individual-level data, such as privacy constraints. We develop mixed-integer optimization formulations and scalable approximate algorithms for several classes of graphical models. Unlike standard high-dimensional analyses, our guarantees are governed by new combinatorial notions of signal strength that capture how information propagates across partially observed sources. Extensive simulations further show that integration can substantially improve estimation of source-specific projected graphs relative to separate source methods. Real-data application illustrates the framework's use with partially-observed sources of fatty acid measurements.

papers.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
papers.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

papers.title: CPNav: Calibrated Vision-Language Navigation for Object-Goal Search in Unseen Environments
papers.abstract: Directing a robot to locate a target object in unseen environments remains a central challenge in embodied AI. Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions. We introduce CPNav, a navigation framework that combines collision-aware planning with statistically calibrated VLM action scoring for map-free object-goal navigation. From RGB-D input, CPNav constructs a navigability map, generates collision-free motion primitives, and queries two VLMs for goal detection and action scoring. The resulting scores are calibrated offline via conformal prediction (CP) using oracle actions obtained through a tree-structured exploration procedure with backtracking, providing finite-sample guarantees at a user-specified risk level. The CP layer is model-agnostic and can wrap any VLM policy. Online, calibrated VLM scores guide action selection, while a tree-structured exploration history records alternative actions and allows backtracking. We evaluate CPNav in both simulation and real-world hardware settings. In AI Habitat simulation, compared with the uncalibrated baseline method, CPNav achieves relative SR and SPL improvements of 6.2% and 11.4% on HM3D v0.2, and 12.4% and 8.8% on MP3D, respectively. In real-world deployment on a modified Hiwonder MentorPi robot, the corresponding improvements in SR and SPL are 24.9% and 15.2%, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/practice-lab-ucla/CPnav.

papers.title: Is Token Confidence Just Chain Length? A Signal-Processing Audit of Reasoning Traces
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models answer math problems by writing long chains of thought, and sampling many chains per problem and taking a majority vote raises accuracy at a large cost in generated text. A popular way to cut that cost scores each chain by the model's confidence in each token it writes, where a token is a word or part of a word. The method averages this confidence over a sliding window of 2048 tokens and keeps or stops chains based on the lowest average. We treat the confidence, recorded token by token, as a signal in the sense of audio or radio, and examine the method with standard signal-processing tools such as spectral analysis and statistical tests for detecting a sudden change. We sampled 16 chains for each of 500 problems from two math benchmarks with a small open reasoning model. The windowed-minimum score turns out to measure mostly how long a chain is. Ranking chains by length alone does as well as or better than the confidence score, and once length is accounted for the score carries no information about correctness. Signal processing explains why: the minimum of a longer stretch of a slowly drifting signal is lower by chance alone, and the confidence signal drifts slowly enough that this effect dominates. The spectrum does hold a small signal that length does not explain, since incorrect chains carry more rapid token-to-token fluctuation, but it is too weak to improve the vote. For stopping chains early, neither the sliding average nor a classical change detector beats the simpler choice of sampling fewer chains.

papers.title: PerfArena: Ranking LLMs by Code Performance
papers.abstract: Industry now relies on LLMs to write a large share of production code. Although that code is mostly, but not always, correct, correctness alone does not determine whether it is fit for repeated and extensive use, which depends on what the code costs in time, memory and energy. Most code-generation benchmarks nonetheless evaluate correctness in isolation, and most performance-oriented benchmarks cover few languages and rarely measure energy consumption. To address this gap, we present PERFARENA, an open-source, reproducible arena that ranks LLMs by the performance of their generated code across multiple languages and competitions. PERFARENA executes the solutions of each LLM on a Unix-like host and reports correctness together with latency, peak memory, and energy consumption. Correctness oracles, performance oracles, profilers, and code-generation workflows are pluggable in PERFARENA, enabling the integration of new judging backends and measurement tools without changing the pipeline. We evaluate PERFARENA on two competitions: CLBGComp, 10 compute-intensive benchmarks from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game, and LeetCodeComp, 99 LeetCode problems whose accepted solutions differ measurably in latency. Currently, PERFARENA holds 9,455 correct and measured solutions from 13 state-of-the-art LLMs across 7 programming languages. Across both competitions, got-6-astra is the only LLM that no other LLM beats significantly in latency, energy consumption, or peak memory, solving 99.7% of LeetCodeComp and 100% of CLBGComp. All PERFARENA leaderboards and measured solutions are publicly available, providing a continuously updated reference that helps developers choose an LLM per language and metric, instead of relying only on correctness rates or pricing.

papers.title: RAGScope: A Leakage-Controlled, Cost-Aware Evidence-Gating Protocol for RAG Hallucination Triage
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems need inexpensive ways to route generated answers: accept low-risk outputs, review uncertain ones, and reserve strong verifiers for the expensive tail. We present RAGScope, a leakage-controlled protocol for evaluating local evidence gates that use only the task input, retrieved context, and answer text. The protocol combines context-grouped splits, fold-scoped preprocessing, group bootstrap intervals, deployment operating points, end-to-end runtime, and explicit source-shift stress tests. On three RAGTruth tasks, the enhanced gate RAGScope-E reaches 0.798 AUROC and 0.660 average precision (AP) in pooled grouped cross-validation. Its pooled AP exceeds ROUGE-L by 0.034 with a 95% context-group interval of [0.002, 0.064], although the AUROC gain is not significant and ROUGE-L remains stronger on data-to-text. At a top-10% review budget, RAGScope-E attains 0.748 precision; accepting the lowest-risk 50% yields 0.141 residual unfaithfulness. RAGScope-E runs in 6.22 ms/example on CPU, versus 145.75 and 223.07 ms/example for the tested DeBERTa-NLI and HHEM settings. A 14,900-example HaluBench stress test exposes the deployment boundary: an in-domain calibrated gate reaches 0.879 AUROC, but leave-source-out calibration averages only 0.466. Target-only calibration recovers to 0.675 AUROC with 100 labels per source and 0.685 with 200. Cheap evidence gates are therefore useful routing components, but learned calibration must be validated and adapted within the target domain.

papers.title: PermVLA: Factorization Order as a Regularizer for VLA Learning
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. We identify factorization order as an overlooked regularization choice and introduce causally anchored permutation (CAP), which samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix. Its auxiliary objective trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known subsets of the same expert chunk, while deployment retains deterministic LTR control. We call this conditional-set augmentation: it creates multiple conditional prediction problems from one expert chunk without adding demonstrations. This discourages reliance on the single chronological prefix used by ordinary teacher forcing. Controlled experiments show that CAP consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the same advantage appearing in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. A diagnostic that measures the expected squared difference between a chunk's joint log likelihood under two reveal orders verifies that CAP training internalizes agreement across reveal orders. These findings position sampled subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives as a general recipe for constructing VLA regularizers, illustrated by an extension to diffusion action generators.

papers.title: From Requirements to Attack Trees: Grounded LLM Agents for Design-Time Security Review
papers.abstract: Design-level security weaknesses can arise from requirements, trust assumptions, missing controls, and data flows before implementation begins. Existing security practices often identify these issues after code is written. We present a multi-agent LLM framework for design-time security analysis from product requirement documents and architecture diagrams. The proposed framework parses architecture diagrams into graph representations, generates misuse and failure cases, constructs attack trees, checks governance and compliance gaps, recommends mitigations, assigns enterprise security-domain tags, and produces a candidate revised architecture recommendation for expert review. The framework does not retrieve from Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) databases at inference time. Instead, it analyzes system behavior, trust boundaries, component interactions, and data-flow assumptions. Misuse cases act as intermediate representations that link findings to system components and attack paths, while a validation and refinement loop filters unsupported findings and improves grounding, traceability, and actionability. We evaluate the framework on a Microsoft reference-labeled threat-modeling example, labeled synthetic PRD--architecture pairs, and two open-ended systems: Berty and Gas Town. The reference-labeled case supports threat-recovery and actionability analysis, while the open-ended cases evaluate validity, noise, traceability, actionability, redundancy, and attack-tree quality. Results show that architecture-informed, misuse-driven reasoning improves review quality compared with single-shot and ablation baselines. Keywords: LLM Multi-Agent Systems, Design-Time Security, Threat Modeling, Vulnerability Discovery, Architecture Diagrams, Security Analysis, Misuse Case Derivation, Attack Trees, Iterative Reasoning, Security Governance.

papers.title: System One Models for Wireless Decision-Making:Applications and Performance Evaluation
papers.abstract: Many wireless control tasks require repeated selection of a single action from a finite feasible set under stringent latency and reliability constraints. While large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as general-purpose decision engines, their autoregressive generation mechanism is not naturally aligned with such bounded control problems. This paper investigates System-One models, which directly learn probability distributions over explicitly defined decision spaces, as a lightweight alternative for wireless decision-making. We formalize their decision structure and learning objective, identify their applicability across physical-layer control, radio resource management, mobility, network slicing, and network operations, and evaluate their practical behavior through representative wireless case studies. Using Jev as a System-One implementation, we benchmark decision quality and client-observed latency against generative LLMs and conventional baselines. In receive-antenna selection, Jev delivers up to an 8.5x reduction in median response latency relative to the evaluated LLMs, although this gain comes with a loss in decision quality compared with stronger task-specific alternatives. More notably, in intent-conditioned RAN slicing, Jev achieves utility comparable to the evaluated LLMs while providing more than a 3.5x reduction in median response latency. Complementary evidence from edge-service orchestration further shows that faster decisions do not necessarily translate into lower end-to-end service latency. These results expose a fundamental quality/latency tradeoff and position System-One models not as replacements for numerical optimization, but as a promising decision interface for latency-sensitive, bounded, and intent-driven wireless control.

papers.title: A Geometrical Approach to Constructing Neural Networks for Perfect Training-set Classification
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a method for constructing a neural network that achieves perfect classification of all samples in a given training set, without taking regularization into account. The network is constructed on-demand, with its layer sizes and neuron parameters determined through a geometrical analysis of the input data, in which separating hyperplanes are created and mapped to neurons with step activation functions. The proposed architecture consists of two hidden layers with distinct roles: inter-class separation and transformation of the data into a linearly separable representation. Inter-class separation requires every bi-chromatic pair of samples belonging to different classes to be separated by at least one hyperplane. We show that when this separation is achieved through a hierarchical partitioning of the data, the leaf nodes of the oblique decision tree, obtained as a byproduct, directly define the neurons of the linear separability layer, whose size is only one neuron greater than that of the inter-class separation layer. Experiments on the MNIST dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves perfect training-set classification, and compact models. The direct correspondence between the decision tree and network neurons enhances interpretability and explainability, while the construction procedure offers opportunities for parallel implementation and improved scalability.

papers.title: Compile as Hypothesis: A Headroom Typology for Prompt Optimization on Real Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Automated prompt compilers search for or rewrite prompts under the implicit assumption that optimization consistently improves downstream task performance. We evaluate this assumption on frontier reasoning models through rigorous paired, same-day measurements. Across four optimizer families (genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA, and ESPO) and eight tasks, structured search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners. However, a discrete structural genome provides essential architectural stability, preventing catastrophic bimodal seed-collapse (where unconstrained search collapses toward the judge floor in 3/5 runs). Through 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we establish a three-dimensional headroom typology: prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or physical token truncation, but successfully resolves protocol and formatting errors. On gpt-6, while free-text reflective search (GEPA) yields a +.14 gain on a task where structured search remains flat, qualitative ablation reveals that ~.035 stems from judge-rubric reconstruction while ~.105 reflects genuine instruction refinement. Our pre-registered AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matches the oracle policy in 5/7 groups and rescues seed-collapse arms with zero regret. Finally, we expose silent backend-mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows and provide automated per-call audit verification tools to ensure empirical evaluation fidelity.

papers.title: Transformer-inspired architectures make machine-learned electron densities accurate and transferable enough to bypass self-consistency
papers.abstract: We introduce machine learning models that accurately predict the electron density, the central variable of density functional theory. They are built on Transformer-inspired architectures, which require little computation per parameter and can therefore be enlarged at low cost. The proposed models, SwinUNETR-V2 and its attention-free counterpart NeXtUNETR, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on QM9, with normalized mean absolute errors in the density averaging 0.075% and 0.046%, respectively. The predicted densities are accurate enough to bypass the self-consistent iteration: a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, the median errors are 0.036 meV in the total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in the forces and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces not only recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization but also successfully drive ab initio molecular dynamics. Fine-tuned on small datasets, both networks also transfer accurately to systems containing elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.

papers.title: Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization
papers.abstract: Quantizing AdamW's optimizer states reduces persistent storage, but quantization errors propagate through the moment recurrences and perturb subsequent adaptive updates. We redesign 4-bit optimizer-state quantization for AdamW from the perspective of \emph{rounding space}: the coordinate in which a quantizer chooses between adjacent reconstruction levels. For the second moment, a local analysis of the quantization cell adjacent to zero shows that small mean state error need not imply small mean preconditioner error at the next step. A one-dimensional quadratic construction further shows qualitatively different optimization dynamics under state-space and preconditioner-space rounding. These results motivate Zero-Inclusive Preconditioner-space Stochastic Rounding (\textbf{ZIP-SR}), which retains zero in the second-moment codebook and computes stochastic-rounding probabilities in preconditioner space. As a complementary route, Zero-Excluding EDEN calibration (\textbf{ZE-EDEN}) uses a zero-excluding second-moment codebook and rescales the quantized second-moment block to mitigate the preconditioner distortion caused by the positive quantization floor. Both configurations use 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) for the first moment, with targeted stochastic rounding of the LM-head first moment during the final 10\% of training. Across GPT- and Llama-style pretraining experiments ranging from \textbf{130M} to \textbf{2.7B} parameters, both methods reduce TorchAO 4-bit AdamW's mean validation-loss gap to 32-bit AdamW at every evaluated model size, with the largest reported gap reduction reaching \textbf{70\%}. In full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, both recipes achieve lower validation loss than TorchAO while remaining close to 32-bit AdamW on downstream tasks.

papers.title: S-GAP: Stealthy Graph Attack Primitives for Graph Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Graph Large Language Models (GraphLLMs) enable powerful semantic understanding and reasoning over Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs), while their semantic reasoning may exhibit vulnerabilities to perturbations in node text and graph structure under adversarial attack evaluation. Existing attacks typically construct textual and structural perturbations in separate stages guided by distinct realization intents. However, this separation results in attack-intent fragmentation, causing semantic incoherence between the two perturbation types, thereby undermining attack stealth and making them easier for GraphLLMs to identify and disregard, ultimately weakening attack effectiveness. To avoid attack-intent fragmentation, we propose the Graph Attack Primitive (GAP), an atomic semantic representation that unifies textual and structural perturbations under a coherent attack intent. By carefully calibrating the semantic composition of a GAP, we can achieve strong attack effectiveness while maintaining sufficient attack stealth. Furthermore, we introduce S-GAP (Stealthy GAP), a multi-agent framework that iteratively refines the semantic content of the GAP. The framework unifies GAP planning and realization and continuously refines this process through surrogate evaluation and textual feedback. Extensive experiments across four datasets, three GraphLLMs, and two attack settings show that S-GAP improves ASR over the strongest baselines by 7.02% on average while producing more relationally plausible perturbations, exposing critical vulnerabilities in current GraphLLMs and motivating more robust defenses.

papers.title: Towards Credible Agent-Based Policy Simulations: Disentangling Opportunities and Preferences in a Financial Inclusion Case Study of Egypt
papers.abstract: Credibility is a central topic for agent-based models intended to support policy-making. Simulations must not only represent the target scenarios and their core dynamics but also demonstrate that their assumptions, parameters, and outputs are empirically grounded and sufficiently accurate for their intended use. This paper addresses this challenge by presenting a general modelling framework, aligned with the Capability Approach, for building credible policy simulations that rely on data and domain-expert knowledge.
